newsitem.title: UK: Bulls and bears bet on the British ballot.
newsitem.headline: Bulls and bears bet on the British ballot.

text.p: The British bond market has barely flinched at the prospect of its first Labour government for 18 years.
But which way will it jump once the voting is over and the new government -- whether Labour or Conservative -- faces some tough policy choices?
Reuters asked 10 London traders and analysts what they would do with a portfolio of 100 million sterling worth of gilts going into the election on Thursday.
Answers diverged dramatically, suggesting investors are not so sure of the Labour victory predicted by opinion polls.
David Boal, Head of JP Morgan GEMMS

"If you're not in the market, get in the market. And if you are in five to 10 years you should either get into 25 years if you agree the market is about to rally. If you want a curve trade, sell five and buy three and ten."
Mark Fox, European fixed income strategist, Lehman

"The problem is that everyone is expecting the same thing -- a post election relief rally in gilts, assuming (Opposition Labour Leader Tony) Blair wins a sizeable majority. So I'd take it all out of gilts and split it between 20 percent in the U.S., 30 percent into Germany, 10 percent in France, 20 in Sweden and 20 in Denmark."
Steve Major, head of bond research, Credit Lyonnais
"I'd keep it in gilts. I think it's good value between six months and one year because that's where the curve is discounting too much tightening."
Gianpaolo Mosconi, bond analyst, Sanwa International

"Ahead of the election we would not get too involved with gilts because we think there might be a bit of a sell-off after the election. The spread with Bunds could go to 195 basis points (from 183 now). I would put a bit of it in the medium term -- seven to 10 years -- as I think the short end could come under pressure."
Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic advisor, BankAmerica

"I'd be inclined to stay in gilts, contingent on Blair getting a moderate majority of around 50 to 100 seats. I'd go for the longer end. The inflation numbers are good so that's positive for that end and if rates do go up inflation expectations will also be positively affected. I'd certainly be beyond 10 years."

Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives, Cooperative Bank "I'd prefer to be relatively flat ahead of Friday -- that takes in the election and the U.S. non-farm payrolls -- and then invest the 100 million sterling afterwards.
"I don't think the election will have any real effect on the market. There would only be a relief rally in gilts if the Conservatives get back in."
Michael Burke, bond strategist, Citibank

"I'd be at the long end of the gilt curve as it offers good relative value. I think there are artificially high spreads over Bunds and Treasuries...and on any election outcome we will see a fairly gilt friendly economic environment."
Andrew Cossor, fixed income analyst, Technical Data

"I like gilts in the medium term and there's no reason to liquidate them. There's the prospect of a quarter-point rate hike which will be good for the market, and also I expect Labour will need to acquire credibility through fiscal tightening. That means they won't need to issue so many gilts. Gilts offer the chance to diversify from EMU risk, at rates well above Bunds."
Craig Shute, fixed income analyst,Bear Stearns

"I'd sell it. The UK markets have performed very well on the belief the Labour Party is going to form the next government with a large House of Commons majority. That's probably going to be the outcome but it's looking like it's going to be a classic case of buy the rumour sell the fact."
Bronwyn Curtis, chief int'l economist, Nomura Int'l "I'd

keep it in there. I think we will have a large, workable majority for Labour. It's looking very attractive again if you look at gilts over Bunds (on yield spreads) at 185 basis points. It's above Italy again."
